Banuba's TINT face analysis and seasonal color analysis gives AI beauty advice. Actually putting on makeup and styling hair are physical jobs that an agent without a body cannot do.
AI video sales agents that run product demos and answer pricing questions are on the market in 2026, but they work only over online channels, not at a door or a street stall.

Door-to-door selling means a solicitor is physically present: cities require permits, a photo ID badge worn while soliciting, and set hours. This assumes a person at the door, but no law says a human must give the product explanation itself.
Cities require background checks and in-person license applications for each person selling door to door, which shows the job depends on face-to-face contact and trust.

John Deere sells retrofit autonomy kits for 8R/9R and 5ML tractors. Farmers control and monitor the machines through the Operations Center mobile app, but people still install the kits and the setup only works with certain equipment and implements.

Center-pivot irrigation can be started, stopped, scheduled and automated through apps such as Valley AgSense, FarmHQ and Agrico Web Control. This only works when a hardware controller has been physically installed on the pivot.

Autonomous tillage only works with John Deere implements fitted with the kits. Most of the work is still done in person: hitching, refuelling, adjusting, fixing breakdowns and tending machines in the field. A software agent can at most send commands through the app on connected equipment.

Deere's autonomous field work is aimed at tillage. Planting and spraying were only stated future goals, and there is no sign of a launched planting product. These systems also depend on robotic tractor hardware, with the farmer overseeing them through the Operations Center app. A software-only agent could at most help with planning and remote monitoring.

Autonomous operation requires camera and autonomy retrofit kits or factory-built autonomy-ready tractors and implements. This means the task depends on physical machinery, and someone has to be there to hitch, load and calibrate the towed implements.

Deere's autonomy was demonstrated pulling a field cultivator on fields that had already been mapped, with obstacle handling done remotely by a human. It is not a turnkey way to run seed drills or manure spreaders. Separately, US rules usually require a certified applicator to apply or supervise restricted-use pesticides.
Agricultural bagging relies on hoppers, tunnels and grain-tank film tubes that are worked by hand at the machine itself. A software-only agent has no way to position boxes or attach bags.
Automatic bag feeders, sewers and heat sealers already open, fill and close bags. That is fixed mechanical automation, not something an AI agent can do through documents, messages or computer use.
Patented bagging gear uses grippers and clamps to physically handle bag mouths, so the task comes down to physical manipulation at the discharge point.
OSHA 1910.266(h) requires an undercut and a backcut on each tree, with enough hinge wood left to control the fall. Both cuts are made by hand with a saw on the standing tree at the stump.
NIOSH FACE reports recommend that fellers drive felling wedges on trees with back lean. This is physical manipulation done on site, so a software-only agent with no robotic body cannot do it.
State and agency chainsaw and tree-felling safety programs built on 29 CFR 1910.266 treat this as hands-on chainsaw and axe work done in the felling zone.
A choker setter is a logger who attaches cables to logs by hand so skidders or skylines can haul them out. The work is done in person on steep cutover ground.
A choker is a steel cable noose that the worker wraps around the end of a log and tightens before the turn is yarded. This requires handling the rigging physically.

Oregon OSHA cable-yarding rules require rigging crew members on site to carry transmitters while chokers are set, and a lone choker setter must stay in clear view of the yarder operator. These rules assume a human is physically present.
OSHA 1926.451(f)(7) requires that scaffolds be erected, moved, dismantled or altered only under the supervision of a competent person, by trained and experienced employees whom that person selects.
A competent person must inspect scaffolds before each shift and after any event that could affect their structural integrity. This needs someone physically on site.
OSHRC enforcement shows citations issued when a scaffold was erected with no competent person present. This confirms the human supervision and liability requirement.

Installing flat-roof insulation and vapor barriers is manual work on the roof: laying rigid boards in a staggered pattern, driving fasteners or placing adhesive beads, and taping or sealing the vapor-retarder seams. The fastener and adhesive layout is set by the product and the spec.

The roofing robots now on the market (for example Renovate Robotics' Rufus) lay shingles on sloped residential roofs and still need a human operator. No production system for installing insulation boards on flat roofs was found, and a software-only AI agent has no physical way to do this work.

Licensing applies to the roofing contractor business (state or local, often above a dollar threshold), not to an individual worker installing insulation. A human does not have to sign off on this specific task.

State 811 centers take locate requests online. The request needs contact details, the work address, cross streets, the type of work (for example, a fence) and the equipment to be used, and a confirmation email is sent back. A software agent can do all of this on its own.

Before digging, the crew has to check on site that every utility has responded and marked its lines. Buried lines can sit up to 24 inches from the marks, so hand digging near them is advised. That checking and marking work is physical.

Free county GIS parcel viewers show property lines that an agent can look up, but they are not survey grade. A licensed surveyor or physical survey pins are needed to fix the exact fence line on the ground.

On track tampers and liners, the reference chord is a physical wire or cord. Its ends are held on bogies or buggies that are pressed against the rail, so someone has to string, tension and clamp it by hand on the track.

Modern machines use three-point chord measurement with sensors on buggies in front of the machine. Setting it up and attaching it to the rails is a hands-on job at the track, not something software can do.

Automated lining and raising systems, including light-beam chords, automate the measurement once installed. Mounting and attaching the reference system to the rails is still done physically by the operator.

Patents describe automatic jack-extension and mast-leveling systems that run on the rig's own sensors and hydraulics. A person still has to position the truck on site, and nothing here is driven by a software-only agent.
A federal drill rig operator job posting requires a Commercial Driver's License with air brake, tanker and trailer-towing endorsements, so a licensed human has to drive the truck-mounted rig.
A Driller industry column says most US states require a CDL to drive drilling equipment and a state well driller's license to drill.

FieldStockPro is an AI-powered inventory tool for trade businesses. It sets loadout templates for each vehicle, monitors stock on each truck and sends automated restock recommendations when parts fall below minimum levels. Technicians still scan parts in and out by hand.
Fieldcode Plus shows part availability by van and technician, sends low-stock alerts and generates reorder suggestions automatically. This covers the digital tracking and reordering steps.

Field service stock systems deduct parts used on jobs and send replenishment alerts. They depend on data entered at the physical van and job site, and sources warn that tools get abandoned when data entry is cumbersome. Physical counting, picking and loading stay with the human.
Boston: only a contractor with a valid, non-expired Massachusetts trade license may pull a Gas Permit and do any work installing or replacing gas lines or pipes.
Angi, a secondary consumer source, says gas grill line installations need permits that are usually pulled by certified plumbers, typically costing $100-$300.

The core of the task is hands-on work at the site: cutting, threading and fitting pipe, making the connections and leak-testing gas and water lines. An agent with no robotics cannot do this. It can only help with small side jobs like looking up code or ordering parts.
O*NET lists 'position or align components for assembly, manually or using hoists' as a core task of Engine and Other Machine Assemblers, along with setting and checking part clearances.

Assembler postings describe hands-on work: moving parts by hand or overhead crane, putting shims between parts to realign or level them, and checking alignment and clearance with micrometers and gauges. This needs a physical body, which a software-only agent does not have.

Mechanical assembler duties include positioning and securing engine block components with wrenches, hammers and power hoists, and running crane or hoist equipment. All of this is physical manipulation; an agent could at most help by looking up blueprints or alignment specs.
Trimming molded fiberglass parts is commonly done by hand. Automating it needs vision- and laser-guided robots, which is physical robotics and not something a software AI agent can do.
The UK occupational standard treats trimming composite mouldings with hand tools (cutting, sanding, drilling) as a hands-on, physical skill.
Automated trimming that does exist uses 5-axis CNC robot trimming centres, which is physical machinery and outside the reference technology.

Machines that change bobbins automatically (doffing and donning) are mechanical devices. Otherwise, putting empty bobbins on spindles and taking full ones off is done by hand. Neither is something a software-only AI agent can do.
Each spindle can have a mechanical gripper that lifts off the full bobbin and places an empty one. This is physical handling done by machinery, not by digital agents.
Automatic loading and unloading of bobbins on spinning and winding machines needs dedicated hardware, which shows the task is physical manipulation.
Graining metal means physically wiping thinned ink onto the surface with cheesecloth, combs or rollers, then lacquering it. Only hands or machinery can do this; software has no part in it.
Industrial graining transfers ink with etched plates and rollers. That is physical printing equipment, not something an AI agent can do through software.
Faux-grain technique depends on hand skill applied to wet glaze, such as dragging and rocking a graining tool, which takes practice to get right.

Building a box assembly jig means physically cutting a flat base and fixing rails or stops precisely square. That is bench work an agent without a body cannot do. It can only help with the layout and dimensions.
Assembly jigs use physical spacer strips and locating stops lined up with the slat ends. The worker has to place and check these by hand.
Box assembly jigs are physical tools that hold the sides upright so they can be glued and nailed. The work is hands-on, and no licence or legal sign-off is needed.

Yokogawa's eLogBook moves control-room logsheets into a digital system. It records operator observations and manually captured process data, supports shift handover, and can start maintenance requests, so the logs are machine-readable.

Pertamina's LEADS system at the Jambaran Tiung Biru gas plant uses an LSTM autoencoder on historical process data. It detects anomalies and sends early warnings, including flagging nomination (demand) changes and start-ups.

In a Baker Hughes/C3 AI compressor deployment, AI detected over 88% of anomalous events and cut alarms by 99%. Operators still confirm and act on the detections, and plant OT data is usually on restricted networks.

Air Liquide has run multivariable model predictive control (Yokogawa PACE) on its air separation units for over 20 years. The units adapt on their own to customer demand and power prices, and the vendor reports no operator intervention was needed in steady state or during load changes. The work an agent could take over is mostly this DCS/APC supervision, and dedicated control software already does much of it.

Field operators do rounds, inspecting equipment by sight, sound and smell and reading local gauges. They make local adjustments to valves, dampers and controllers, which is physical work an agent without a body cannot do.
ASU operators handle start-up and shut-down as well as preventive and corrective maintenance. These are the hands-on, non-routine parts of controlling the equipment.

In retreading, stitching means pressing a roller onto the newly placed tread to push air out of the bond line and make the bond layer an even thickness. It is a physical step done by hand or by machine.
Mechanical tire stitching machines exist. This shows the step is done by physical machinery, not by software agents with no body.
Older equipment for putting camelback onto tire casings is also mechanical, so the task is about physically handling rubber and the casing.

Marine autopilots already hold a course on their own: heading mode keeps a compass heading, and track mode holds a GPS course over ground by correcting for cross-track error. Operators still hand-steer in congested or tricky water, and these are dedicated onboard control systems, not something a software-only AI agent can normally operate.
Garmin documents autopilot heading-hold and route-following modes that run through the boat's own onboard hardware.
Carrying paying passengers on small vessels requires a USCG OUPV or Master credential held by a human operator. This requires sea time, an exam, a physical and a drug test.

The only gutter-cleaning automation found was a hardware robot, the iRobot Looj. It is now discontinued and was driven by a person on site who had to place it in the gutter. Software agents with no body can't do this.
The Looj was remote-controlled or ran on its own only after a person put it into the gutter. Clearing debris means physically working on the roofline, so someone has to be there.

MSHA rule 30 CFR 57.3200 says hazardous ground must be taken down or supported in the underground workplace before anyone else works or travels in the area. Taking down loose ground is physical work done on site.

30 CFR 57.3202 requires a scaling bar when scaling is done by hand. 30 CFR 57.3401 requires the mine operator to designate people experienced in examining and testing for loose ground, which means a qualified person must be physically present and accountable.

Commission case law says loose ground is judged by on-site tests such as sounding, visible fractures and popping noises. These checks require someone physically there to sense and handle the rock. A software-only agent with no body cannot pry rock or move it.

Funeral-home software such as Memorion already covers scheduling, documentation, invoicing and workforce management, with an AI assistant whose output staff review. Search results showed no AI tools for funeral-home hiring decisions or for supervising staff.

In Kansas, each funeral establishment must always be under the charge and personal supervision of a licensed funeral director, who is responsible for staff conduct. No funeral arrangement may proceed without a licensed director or assistant director present.

Virginia requires a licensed manager of record for each funeral establishment, named on the establishment's license. Wisconsin requires a licensed funeral director in charge with full supervision of funeral directing and embalming.

Vendors sell AI colony-counting and plate-reading tools for water and environmental monitoring, such as Copan PharmaLab, Kikkoman CCS and Tailin ASC-2000Pro. They automate only the image-reading step, which happens after a human has physically sampled, plated and incubated the material. Accuracy figures come from the vendors and have not been independently validated.

Under state programs based on the EPA drinking-water lab certification manual, compliance microbiology analyses must be done by approved analysts. In Kentucky that means 30 days of supervised bench training, 60 more days of bench experience and passing proficiency tests. Ohio adds that each analyst must analyze at least 10% of routine samples. The requirements were read from state documents, not the federal manual itself.

UKAS has accredited automated colony counters such as Synbiosis ProtoCOL for counting microbes in water. That is still instrument-assisted counting inside an accredited lab workflow run by people, not autonomous testing.

Jail management systems already handle inmate movements, headcounts, cell checks, shift notes and incident reports digitally. Vendors list AI Copilot and generative AI features, which suggests that data entry and drafting can be automated.

Some analysts propose AI analytics that combine camera and sensor feeds into single incident logs. The source is an opinion piece, not a tested deployment, and officers still observe events on the unit in person.

Correctional policy requires each staff member who witnesses an incident to write their own observation report, sign it and send it to a supervisor for review and signature. This means a human must give the account and attest to it.

O*NET lists 'Use nondisciplinary tools and equipment, such as a computer' as a task for Correctional Officers and Jailers (33-3012.00). Related job descriptions show the equipment includes radios, intercoms, phones, restraints and central control booth equipment, which are used on site inside the facility.

Jail management software already automates parts of the computer work, such as syncing arrest reports into the jail system, filling in charges automatically, sending warrant alerts and checking reports with AI. Officers still enter data, check it and act on it in person.
Officers in control centers watch inmates using CCTV and computer tracking systems. Much of the equipment use is tied to physical presence and live security operations inside the facility.
AI tools such as Quorum's Quincy and ChatGPT prompt packs for congressional staff draft talking points, meeting briefs and media messaging. The legislator still delivers them and negotiates.
PolicyPage drafts one-page legislative meeting briefs, with citations, tailored to a specific legislator. This is preparation support only, not the representation itself.
Parliamentary mandates and votes are personal and cannot be delegated (for example, Article 79.6 of the Spanish Constitution). Representing a party is tied to an elected, accountable human.

Purpose-built exit-lane systems at airports already raise real-time alerts to security staff when someone walks the wrong way through an exit lane (Kaba at McCarran; CheckVideo ExitSentry). That covers only one narrow type of breach and depends on fixed sensors and cameras, not a general AI agent.

Breach notification is tied to the screener's physical work at the checkpoint, such as following people who breach security until police arrive. The breach is usually spotted in person, and the alert is a quick radio or verbal call, so an agent adds little unless it has the camera and radio feeds.

Under 49 CFR 1544.405, no one may perform a screening function unless qualified. Checkpoint procedures are restricted as sensitive security information, which limits an agent's access to checkpoint systems.

O*NET lists this task for Fitness and Wellness Coordinators, together with a related duty to manage and train staff of wellness specialists, health educators or fitness instructors. The work combines people management with in-person oversight.

Gym instructor-management software such as NetGym automates instructor scheduling, substitute requests, communication and analytics on instructor behaviour. These are administrative sub-steps an agent could run.

AI tools for gyms forecast class demand, balance instructor workloads and link instructor-level factors to member retention. They support supervisory decisions, but the evidence that they give useful coaching feedback in practice is thin.

In 2026, AI recruiting agents can source, screen, reach out to candidates, schedule and run structured AI interviews (for example Paradox and HireVue) with little human involvement. Vendors still recommend that a human review final hiring decisions.
Vendor buyer guides describe autonomous hiring agents covering top-of-funnel steps. Supervising staff day to day, coaching them and managing their performance on the store floor stays a human job.

NYC Local Law 144 requires bias audits and candidate notice for automated employment decision tools but does not ban them and does not require a licensed human to sign. This is a regulatory burden, not a rule that a human must do the work.

Banks report that agentic AI coding and legacy-code work runs 2 to 20 times faster for some tasks (Citi). Morgan Stanley's DevGen.AI reviewed 9 million lines of legacy code and turned them into plain-English specifications. Agents can do the code changes but did not take over model ownership.

US model risk guidance (SR 11-7, reportedly replaced in 2026 by SR 26-2) requires model development to be documented, validation to be independent, and human governance structures to approve model changes. Sources disagree on whether GenAI and agents are inside its scope, and I could not check the Fed's own text.
One bank's AI coding trial reported up to 20% less boilerplate coding effort, including code review and refactoring. That points to large help on sub-steps, with humans still reviewing the work.

Atlassian's Jira Delivery Agent (Rovo) analyzes Jira spaces and connected data to report on progress. It runs inside automation rules and can be set up for different audiences, from team summaries to executive updates.

Atlassian ships automation templates for Daily Standup, Delivery Health Check and Stakeholder Status Summary. They compile progress, risks and completed work and post the result to Confluence or Slack, which automates the recurring parts of carrying out a communication plan.

Atlassian's 'Harper' workshop shows how to build a custom agent that writes project-health, milestone and risk summaries for PMOs, executives and team leads. A human still decides stakeholder priorities, handles sensitive messages and leads the live meetings.

By 2026, vendors were selling agentic AI for clinical data management. Examples: Veeva's Study Builder Agent configures EDC forms, visits and edit checks from a protocol; Hexaware's agents propose CRFs and validation rules; Clinion's assistant answers natural-language questions about live study and operational data. These tools could support data-driven review of processes and technology, but the efficiency gains are still mostly vendor claims.

Hexaware's agentic CDM offering automates sub-steps such as CRF design, CDISC mapping and edit-check suggestions. That shows agents can analyze workflows and suggest changes, but humans still decide what to adopt.

Under ICH E6(R3), the sponsor keeps ultimate responsibility and must run risk-based oversight of computerized systems and data governance. Process changes therefore need human review and approval before rollout, although the task of suggesting revisions does not itself require a human signature.

Veeva announced its Study Builder Agent on September 24, 2026. Veeva says it configures EDC forms, visits and edit check rules directly from a study protocol, and automates testing, including generating test data. Early-adopter access is planned for December 2026, so it is not yet generally available in October 2026. The time savings come from the vendor and have not been independently checked.

A Medidata-sourced opinion piece from April 2026 says AI can cut study build timelines from 10 to 12 weeks down to a few days, and that it can flag common data inconsistencies and suggest edit checks. This is promotional commentary.

Clinical trial databases covered by 21 CFR Part 11 must be validated, with defined roles that include an approver. Failing to validate can lead to regulatory citations. This means a qualified, accountable person still has to review and sign off on the database and edit-check validation before go-live. The source is a secondary university guide, not the regulation itself.

Commercial AI tools (TuMeke, ConductVision, Human Focus) already score RULA, REBA and the NIOSH lifting equation automatically from workplace video. Agreement with expert human reviewers has been reported as good, but it has not been fully established.

Studies of the reliability of AI video-based REBA against human raters show the agent can do the analysis step, but a human still has to check the results. Recording the video and taking force or anthropometric measurements on site needs a person to be there.
No ergonomics certificate (such as the BCPE's CPE) is legally required to do ergonomic analysis, and the search found no rule that a licensed person must sign the assessment.

ClimatePolicyGen (2026) is a multi-agent framework that analyzes environmental, socio-economic and infrastructure data to produce climate policy recommendations. It is validated only by automated metrics and has not been deployed by a government.

Research benchmarks test AI agents on climate policy reasoning, including treaty interpretation and adaptation policy, which shows they can do the main analytical sub-steps but have not yet been shown to replace an analyst from start to finish.

Ready-made agents already market themselves as environmental policy advisors that produce policy recommendations, so the drafting step can be delegated. Working out what is politically feasible and persuading stakeholders still depends on human judgment and trust.

Instrument vendors build diagnostics into their own software. Shimadzu's Nexera spots flow and pressure faults, purges the pumps and re-injects the sample on its own, but it still stops and passes the problem to a person when the fault persists.

Research systems with several AI agents watch instruments and keep troubleshooting histories for lab QC. These are proteomics and mass-spectrometry setups, not HPLC, and one agent's precision was low (0.41), so it raised many false alarms. I found no independent test of an AI agent fully diagnosing real HPLC faults from start to finish.

US drug-manufacturing rules (21 CFR 211.68) require automated and electronic equipment to be routinely calibrated, inspected or checked under a written program, with records kept. In practice, fixes such as replacing seals, fixing leaks and swapping columns are done by hand at the instrument.

Industry guides and vendors describe AI drafting GxP SOPs, flagging unclear wording and tracking guideline changes to find affected SOPs. They stress that a human must review the drafts, because AI cannot know what actually happens on the floor, so process owners have to supply the facts.
Vendor tools such as CaseMark sell GMP SOP generation workflows and claim the first draft takes minutes instead of 20-40 hours. This is unverified marketing.

Under 21 CFR 211.22, the quality control unit must approve or reject procedures that affect identity, strength, quality and purity, and its procedures must be in writing. This means a human from that unit has to approve the work.

A randomized trial found an AI agent that reviewed primary-care registries for hereditary cancer risk and handled genetic-counseling follow-up for more than 3,000 patients performed about as well as the manual approach. A 2025 review says AI's potential for population health management is still largely untapped and calls for rigorous evaluation.

A 2026 JMIR feasibility study used an agentic AI platform on a claims database to estimate the prevalence of six conditions. This shows agents can run the data-analysis step of an evaluation, but the work still needs validation and access to protected data.

ACPM's privileging standards and ABPM's competencies list health services planning and evaluation, and evaluating a health system's delivery of preventive services, as specialty competencies. Employers expect board-certified physicians in these roles, but no law requires a licensed person to sign this kind of analytic work.

Endoscopy technicians do hands-on maintenance work. They leak-test and take apart scopes to the manufacturer's specs, pull scopes that fail from service, check machine water pressure and change filters. An agent with no body can't do any of this.

Software only supports the work. Tracking systems record a device's damage, test results and repair history, and a deep-learning model reviewing borescope video of working channels caught 91.4% of the problems endoscopists found. That model only flags scopes for a person to check and send for repair; it doesn't do the inspection or the repair itself.

An agent could take on the paperwork side: filling in repair logs, keeping records, sending scopes out for repair and coordinating with the manufacturer. That is a small part of the time, while the physical inspection, troubleshooting and repair make up most of it.

Healthcare learning platforms already use AI to build role-based compliance courses from policy documents. They also offer AI roleplay for sensitive patient conversations and simulated patients for training patient-support staff, which covers drafting materials and running practice sessions.
AI authoring tools turn uploaded policy and regulatory documents into structured training outlines and draft content, including HIPAA training for front-line patient interactions.

The CMS patient-rights rule (42 CFR 482.13) sets the hospital's grievance process and the staff training required for restraint and seclusion. Searches found no rule that a licensed person must deliver guest-relations or patient-rights training. The hospital still has to approve and stand behind its policies, so a human reviews the content.

Weather sealing is hands-on rooftop work. The installer sets flashing, fastens the mounts and injects sealant through the mount ports until it comes out, removing the mount to seal by hand if needed. An agent without a body cannot do any of this.

Installers fill the pilot holes with MS polymer, silicone or butyl sealant and then seat the flashing. Software can only help with the edges of the job, such as looking up which sealant a manufacturer specifies.
Roof penetrations are checked in rough-in and final building inspections, and permits name licensed contractors. However, no law specifically requires that a licensed human apply the sealant.

LoopWorks MRF OS scale-house app records gross, tare and net weight, material type, contamination, supplier and driver in one form, and traces each ton from the scale through the baler to the outbound load. Log capture and reconciliation can be done digitally, but someone on site still has to confirm what physically arrived or left before the log is accepted.
AMCS Scale House connects directly to scales to weigh incoming and outgoing material and feeds transaction records, so an agent working through software could keep the logs from system data.
ReMatter's scale-ticket product automatically takes pictures of scales for compliance documentation, which cuts down manual ticket transcription.

Manual J load calculations are routinely done in software such as Wrightsoft Right-J. The software handles the math and recalculates loads as inputs change, and vendors say many contractors now use AI heat load tools. Software still cannot give accurate loads if the user does not apply Manual J procedures correctly, so a human has to review the inputs and assumptions.

Many US jurisdictions require a Manual J report with the permit, and it must come from ACCA-approved software. The search found no general rule that a licensed engineer must sign it, and enforcement varies widely by locality.

Remote services sell permit-ready Manual J calculations made from plans and owner-supplied data. This shows the calculation can be done without being on site, but it depends on accurate measurements of the home's envelope, windows and insulation.

Library technician job profiles describe first-level, often in-person troubleshooting of copiers, printers, microform readers and AV equipment, with harder problems sent on to IT. Clearing jams, swapping cables and replacing parts takes hands-on work that an agent without a body cannot do.

Products shipping by 2026, such as TeamViewer Tia and the Ivanti and ServiceNow service-desk agents, find and fix software and endpoint problems on their own. That covers the computer part of the task: remote diagnosis, fixes, logging tickets and contacting vendors. Independent data on how often they fix things without help is still thin.
O*NET lists this as a core library technician task. No licence or sign-off is needed, but the agent would need remote-management access to library machines, and it may not have that.

Hotel AI tools such as Accor's ALL Concierge and Yanolja's AI concierge already answer property questions, help with bookings and in-stay requests, and give recommendations. Yanolja lets human staff take over a conversation in real time when needed. Accor reports more than 1 million guest conversations in its pilot.
Canary Technologies runs AI voice and text agents for the front desk, concierge and reservations. They both answer guest questions and act on requests through hotel systems.
Vendors say LLM agents handle 80% or more of guest messages and up to 80% of call volume. These figures are unverified marketing claims, and unusual or in-person cases still go to staff.

Bedside voice AI products like OrbitaASSIST already take spoken patient requests (for example 'tell the nurse I need a pillow' or 'I've fallen'), then triage, prioritize and route them to care-team devices. This covers the call-answering and needs-intake sub-steps.

AI virtual triage is used alongside nurse triage call centers to collect symptoms and prioritize requests. In a 54,587-encounter study it cut unnecessary consultations, which shows automated needs-assessment works for remote, verbal interactions.

Many calls still need an aide at the bedside to see the patient (falls, incontinence, pain, confusion, patients who can't speak). A human therefore performs essential steps, but no license or signature is required to answer call lights.
Surgical positioning means physically moving the patient, keeping the body aligned, and padding pressure points. RNs direct technicians and assistants, who do the physical moving.
Positioning is a shared responsibility of the perioperative team. The RN applies the positioning devices and the surgeon chooses the position, so licensed professionals stay accountable for the work.

Pressure injury is the most common positioning complication. Preventing it depends on hands-on placement of padding and devices, and OR documentation records skin condition and devices used. A software-only agent could help only with that documentation.

Fiery Scribe, announced in March 2026, is an agent that watches an email inbox for print job requests, works out the job specifications and loads the jobs into Fiery Command WorkStation. That is automated intake of job requirements.

AI quoting tools can read customer files uploaded to web-to-print portals and pull out dimensions, page count, orientation and color space. This automates part of the requirements discussion. The claims come from vendors and have not been independently verified.

Chat-based intake agents for print shops list missing specs, write follow-up questions and handle exceptions. Talks about binding plans still usually involve physical samples or dummies and judgment about the shop's own equipment, which is why a human stays in the loop.

University of Washington researchers built multi-agent AI that generates life-cycle inventories and carbon footprints for electronics from just a product name. Error ran 5-19%, close to expert LCAs, but it covers only cradle-to-gate emissions, not a full LCA.

Commercial LCA tools (Makersite, Sphera, One Click LCA) use AI to fill data gaps, match bills of materials to background databases, import files through an AI agent and run scenarios at scale. Primary data from suppliers is still needed.

Consultancy summaries of ISO 14044 (I could not check the clause text) say that when an LCA supports a public comparative claim, an independent expert panel must review it. For other studies a single independent expert may review it. No licence is needed to conduct an LCA, so a human reviewer is needed only in some cases.

Cistern sizing for rainwater harvesting can already be done with existing calculators and spreadsheet methods: roof catchment area, rainfall data and a water-demand balance. An agent can find the rainfall data online, run these calculations, and write the specifications and narrative documents.

Landscape architects are expected to calculate how much rainwater a project can reuse and what size cisterns it needs, using the project's annual rainfall (LEED context). This is analytical, desk-based work that an agent could largely do.

Technical submissions for permits or construction must carry a licensed landscape architect's seal and signature. Greywater systems may also fall under separate plumbing or health codes, so a licensed human still has to review and sign the work.
AI-CMMS tools only predict boiler faults and generate work orders with suggested parts and timing. A human still does the physical repair.
In Michigan, boiler repair needs a permit from the state boiler division, and permits go only to licensed boiler repairers. Unlicensed workers must be directly supervised by a licensed person.
In NYC, some boiler and burner work must be done by a Licensed Oil Burner Installer or a Licensed Master Plumber, under permits issued to licensed tradespeople.

Vendors describe AI connected-worker platforms (Augmentir, IFS/Poka) that turn videos, PDFs and notes into step-by-step digital work instructions, track training and skills matrices, and show KPI dashboards to managers. That speeds up the documentation and tracking parts of training and supervision. These are vendor claims, not independent evidence.

Augmentir says its AI skills matrix lets managers see their team's skill gaps and act on them. That is decision support, but a human supervisor still oversees the line on the shop floor and demonstrates the procedures.

Federal OSHA has no single general-industry rule requiring supervisor training, so a human signature is not generally required. Training best practice still calls for hands-on practice and workers showing in person that they can do the task, which needs someone physically present.

In 2026 OpenTable says its voice-AI partners have seated 3 million diners. It also reports about 450,000 monthly users for its Concierge AI assistant, which shows routine dinner booking by AI is already common.
AI concierge and voice agents such as Inhotel Golf Assistant and Courserev book golf tee times from live availability and guest preferences, and can put players on waitlists for open slots.

Google Duplex showed AI phoning businesses to make reservations, so venues without online booking can also be reached by an agent. Businesses could opt out of these calls, though, which limits coverage.

Commercial AI CAM tools exist that work from CAD models. Siemens NX AI feature recognition finds holes, pockets, slots and contours, then suggests machining strategies. CloudNC CAM Assist generates 3 and 3+2-axis strategies. Cimatron's CAM agent, shown at IMTS 2026, reads part geometry and the tool library to produce complete 3-axis toolpaths. These are vendor claims, and fully autonomous end-to-end process planning is still mostly in research (TUM AI4CADCAM and TU Darmstadt autonomIQ, both running through late 2026).

Siemens NX AI feature recognition uses machine learning to classify features in 3D models, and the CAM system then proposes toolpaths. A machinist still has to check the plan against the shop's own machines, fixtures and stock, and against physical sample parts that may have no CAD model.

A third-party licensing site, not an official government source, reports that states such as Delaware do not require a state license for machinists. Employers set requirements such as NIMS credentials and apprenticeships, so no law requires a human to sign off on a process plan.
Vendors say AI tools can check product bills of materials for errors in part numbers, revisions and sourcing. That is the main sub-step of checking whether a materials list is accurate.
AI takeoff and material-list tools such as Beam AI and 2by4.ai produce line-item lists, but the vendors still keep a human expert to check accuracy before the list is used.
Home Depot's AI Blueprint Takeoffs tool generates complete material lists and quotes, and a human Pro team member reviews the scope with the customer before the estimate goes out.

2026 agent systems such as ArtiCAD and ToolCAD turn text or image descriptions into editable CAD parts and assemblies, including multi-part assemblies with moving parts. That covers the drafting and modelling steps of designing a repair aid.

The ArtisanCAD authors (July 2026) note that text-to-CAD agents still struggle when design intent is vague or underspecified. Shop-floor repair aids are usually specified that loosely, so a human has to measure on site, try out prototypes and correct the design.

Industrial exemptions, such as Texas Occupations Code §1001.057, generally let employees design tools and equipment for their own company's facilities without a PE licence. A sealed design is required mainly for structural or load-bearing items in some places, such as Ontario after it repealed its exemption.

Sources from 2026 describe agentic marketing systems that take a high-level goal and plan, run and adjust campaigns across channels. Humans still set the goals, budget, brand voice and compliance limits, and they oversee the strategy.
Industry reporting expects marketing operations to be run more and more by multi-agent systems, with human marketers keeping strategy and oversight while agents handle execution at scale.

Vendor guides describe AI marketing agents that create content, sequence campaigns and optimise them in real time. These are vendor claims, not independently verified, and none show agents formulating marketing policy or directing people without a human.

USDA AMS released a free Log Truck Route Planner in March 2026. Its log allocator assigns logs from forests to mills at the lowest cost, and its truck scheduler builds trip plans from the user's delivery requests.

Trimble LogForce links forest owners, haul contractors and mill receivers. Planners use it to split orders into loads, send loads to trucks, manage daily and weekly schedules and message the other parties.

An ORTEC case study describes a timber producer that switched from manual planning to optimized routing, load building and a driver app with electronic proof of delivery. This suggests the digital coordination steps can be automated. Confirming informal deals with small haulers and mills by phone, and checking log grades in the yard, still falls to a human.

The machines that automate dog bathing (PuppyWash and patented washing and brushing enclosures) are physical robotic devices. They are not software agents, and a human still has to load and handle the animal, so a software-only AI agent can't do this task.
Patents for automatic dog washing and brushing describe tubs, brushes, sprayers and motors. Bathing and grooming are hands-on physical work with live animals.
AI-driven wash-cycle adaptation (Woofwoof Lux) is built into dedicated hardware. A software-only agent operating a computer can't reach it or do the work.

AI video tools available now, such as Synthesia (avatar videos built from a script, at scale) and Runway (generating and editing scenes), can produce substantial parts of corporate video products from a written brief. They are weaker on creative range and pre-production.

AI digital asset management systems transcribe, auto-tag and index video libraries, and offer rights and licensing workflows (for example Veritone, Bynder and Canto). That automates much of running a film library and controlling distribution, but tags often lack campaign or channel context, so a human still reviews them.

AI video platforms automate transcription, scene and face detection, and tagging for searching and distributing video assets. Live filming of real events, executives and facilities still needs crews on site, and distribution decisions that affect the brand need human approval.
Agent systems can already turn an incident report into a draft response plan with actions, owners and deadlines, but they are mainly research prototypes, and human review is the usual design.
Vendors offer no-code agent templates that update evacuation plans and coordinate with emergency services. These cover the documentation part of contingency planning.

OSHA 29 CFR 1910.38 makes the employer responsible for the emergency plan, choosing and training evacuation staff, and reviewing the plan with employees. This is work done by people in the workplace and on site, so it can't be fully delegated to an agent.

In 2026 KnowBe4 launched AI Defense Agents (AIDA), including an Orchestration Agent that it says fully automates administration of security awareness training programs and a content agent that builds custom training. These are vendor claims.
Adaptive Security's platform uses generative AI to create personalized security training content and simulations. This is also a vendor claim.

State security-officer rules often require classroom hours taught by licensed or certified instructors. Florida allows live online delivery only when Class DI instructors teach from a physical location in Florida.

Generative AI tools already draft, update and rebuild manufacturing SOPs and work instructions from source material. Vendors say subject-matter experts must review the output and check it against how the work is actually done on the floor before it becomes official.

A patent describes a generative model trained on libraries of industrial process specifications (SOPs, work cell layouts) that turns natural-language descriptions into draft process specifications. This makes the 'develop' part of the task largely automatable.

OSHA 1910.147 requires the employer to inspect each energy-control procedure at least once a year and certify it. The inspection must be done by an authorized employee who watches workers carry out the procedure and talks with them. This means the 'enforce' part needs a human on site and a human who is accountable.

Regulatory horizon-scanning products (for example FinregE's 'Regulatory Operating System') already watch for new regulatory developments. They link that intelligence to policy, control and implementation workflows, so most of the monitoring and summarising can be automated.
Vendors such as CUBE say the hard part is deciding which changes actually matter to a firm's products and policies. That relevance judgement still needs human context and review.
AI tools can process large volumes of outside material and find patterns faster. Human judgement is still needed to supply context and to answer 'so what, now what, who owns it'.

Vendors describe CAPA agents that classify nonconformances, link related events, assign action priority from AIAG/VDA severity, occurrence and detection scores, and draft root-cause suggestions and corrective-action recommendations. Their capability claims are unverified marketing.
An industry guide for FDA-regulated biopharma says AI does not write CAPAs or decide on corrective actions. Qualified people review and decide, so a human review step is still needed.

In regulated QMS settings, a named person in the company must approve and sign quality documents and CAPA. This is an approval duty inside the company, not a licence needed to make the recommendation.

O*NET lists this as a task for Geological Technicians. Related tasks for the same job include taking part in exploratory drilling and well-logging surveys and collecting or preparing solid and fluid samples, which means physical fieldwork.
AI and ML workflows already automate main desk sub-steps of CO2 storage site work, such as seismic horizon and fault interpretation, filling gaps in well data and building reservoir property models.

A CCS site assessment workflow that combines well and seismic reservoir properties was designed to be as automated as possible and was applied across more than 6,000 sq km. Compiling existing data is largely digital work.

Minnesota DNR: when work in public waters is done without a permit, enforcement can include a civil restoration order, and the area hydrologist prepares these orders. An agent can draft such legal documents from templates, statutes and case facts, but the agency issues them and they can be contested in hearings.

Under Minn. R. 6115.0255, the commissioner or agent reviews the evidence, including evidence from the landowner, inspects the site if needed and makes the determination. That requires a human on site and a human decision.

In a real case (Maple Lake, 2015), a conservation officer and an area hydrologist investigated a complaint in person: cattails had been removed and sand and fabric placed below the ordinary high water level. The investigation depended on field visits and talking with the landowner.

Reviews describe AI tools for teachers, such as MagicSchool and Eduaide.AI, that generate worksheets, lesson materials and other teaching resources from a short specification. The sources found did not confirm that these tools make charts or graphic organizers.
Brisk works inside Google and Microsoft documents and webpages. It creates learning materials, changes reading levels and translates content without leaving the browser.

Teacher guides say AI-generated materials should be fact-checked and approved before classroom use, and that private student data should not be uploaded to unapproved tools. This means a human still reviews the output, and some classroom aids are physical items such as posters.

Commercial RFP agents (Folio3, Lyzr) already handle intake, extracting requirements and deadlines, pulling from past winning proposals, drafting, compliance screening and approval routing as separate automated steps.

Vendors say their tools cut RFP response time a lot: Beam AI claims about 40 hours down to 8 per RFP. These are the vendors' own figures, not independent results, but they suggest a human still spends real time reviewing and finishing the work.

Under FAR-based rules, an offer must be signed by a person with authority to bind the offeror, and the contracting officer must confirm that authority. So a human has to commit to the price and terms and sign the bid.
Bloomberg Law built an LLM tool that copy-edits articles to match house style, to cut editors' copy-editing time.
NZ Herald's in-house AI checks grammar and spelling, enforces house style and condenses press releases into articles under an editor's direction, with review before publication.

Newsroom AI policies such as WEHCO's, based on AP standards, require a human editor to review AI output before publication. This is a newsroom norm, not a legal or licensing rule, but it means a human still has to approve or correct the work.

O*NET lists 'Install electrical cables or wire fixtures' as a core task for Lighting Technicians. The work is hands-on: running cable, wiring fixtures and patching them to dimmers at the venue. An agent with no body cannot do it; at most it can look up wiring diagrams or load calculations.
Lighting technicians rig, wire and focus fixtures on site following the designer's plot. In theatre they work under a master electrician, and in film and TV under a gaffer.
Licensing rules differ by US state. Temporary production wiring is often allowed under a limited stage-electrician license or exemption, while permanent wiring requires a licensed electrician.

Software from AI vendors (e.g., Opmed.ai) plans operating-room staffing and changes schedules in real time. This covers the administrative scheduling part of the task, not hands-on clinical direction of the surgical team. Most evidence comes from vendors.

Under CMS teaching-physician rules, the attending surgeon must be physically present for the key or critical parts of surgical procedures done by residents. Supervising the team is an in-person duty that a licensed physician must carry out.

Vendor reports describe AI agents that coordinate hospital staff workflows, such as refilling cancelled slots and updating schedules, without a human involved. These are logistics tasks, not directing clinical staff at the bedside or in the operating room.

Staining means physically moving slides through reagents such as xylene, alcohols, hematoxylin and eosin. Automated stainers can do this, but a person still has to load slide racks and reagent containers. A software agent can only help program protocols (for example, the Histo-Tek SL takes 15 programmable protocols of up to 35 steps), look up procedures or keep records.
Special stains are chemically sensitive and need reagents applied in a set order. That calls for hands-on bench work and quality control, which an agent with no physical body cannot do.

Anatomic pathology counts as high-complexity testing under CLIA, so the people performing it must meet personnel requirements. Several states, including Florida, Nevada and New York, also require a state licence.

Commercial AI deterrence products (Verkada, Alarm.com AID) detect trespassers on camera and give automated spoken warnings that escalate. This covers detection and warnings only. It does not cover physically removing or detaining anyone.
AI video analytics combine human classification with line-crossing detection to give real-time perimeter alerts and automated deterrence. A human still has to respond in person.

When licensed security officers detain or arrest someone, they do it as private citizens under state law. Unlawful detention creates personal liability for false imprisonment, which assumes a human performs the act and answers for it.

AI video and audio alarm verification is sold commercially to cut false alarms. Vendors say 2026 AI agents can assess an intrusion, sound an alarm and write incident reports, but a human operator still decides whether to call police.
Alpha Vision launched an AI security agent at ISC West in March 2026. It offers real-time video analysis, structured incident reporting and natural-language queries to speed up investigations.
Security supervisor postings require responding to alarms in person, doing on-site checks, calming altercations and holding a state security licence.

Gamma's AI agent can take an uploaded budget spreadsheet and build a full formatted budget presentation with charts and category breakdowns. This is the vendor's own claim and was not independently checked.
Microsoft's adoption guidance says its Office Agent (Copilot) can draft budget performance presentations from financial analysis and earlier meeting notes. This is also vendor material.

Security budgets depend on post-coverage minimums written into contracts and on overtime driven by staff turnover. Those inputs come from internal scheduling and payroll data, and a supervisor has to judge them and defend them to management.

AI in fire service is mostly at the dispatch level: computer-aided dispatch adds AI on top of rule-based routing and zoned alerting. That is the dispatcher's job, not the firefighter's on-scene response.
Plans for AI-based dispatch of the nearest fire truck are still proposals. Trucks, drones and people still carry out the physical response.
Responders must hold certification to NFPA 1001 Firefighter I/II, which requires passing practical skills exams plus hazmat and first aid/CPR credentials. This is a human licensing requirement.

Baton Rouge police policy: once a responding officer discovers or identifies a crime scene, that officer immediately becomes responsible for protecting it from contamination. Yellow perimeter tape is the preferred first barrier, so the work is physical and done in person.

Fairfax County police set up two perimeters on site: red 'Crime Scene-Do Not Cross' tape for the inner one and yellow 'Police Line' tape for the outer one. Officers have to place and check both by hand.
Burleson, Texas policy: the officer keeps an entry log recording each person's time in, time out and purpose. This log is the only part of the task software could help with.

Since February 2026, the San Diego County Sheriff has run an AI agent around the clock on its non-emergency line. It decides whether a call goes to a dispatcher or the communication center and points wrong-agency callers to the correct agency. The 71% deflection rate is the vendor's own figure.

AI agents on non-emergency lines in Ontario (Halton's SARA, Owen Sound's CARA) pass emergencies or calls they don't understand to a human. In El Cajon, California, a human still reviews every call the AI handles.

Officers in the field relay information to dispatch by radio and through the mobile data terminal (MDT) linked to the dispatch system (CAD). Some departments forbid using the MDT in place of radio, and high-priority calls go by voice. That means relaying depends on what the officer gathers on scene and on secured police systems.

O*NET describes school bus monitors as helping students board and exit safely, opening and closing doors, operating wheelchair lifts, securing seatbelts and tie-downs, and directing evacuations. All of these need a person physically on the bus.

Existing software, such as RFID card scanning with cloud logging and alerts, only records who gets on and off. It does not direct students, so it covers a small digital part of the job and leaves the in-person direction to a human.
Job postings require monitors to help children get on and off at the right stops in a safe, orderly way, using in-person supervision and behavior management of minors.

Regulator-approved totalisator software works out the pool totals, takeout and winning payouts. A Wisconsin rule requires the mutuel manager to produce a daily summary of pari-mutuel operations as the original record of wagering, so most of the compiling is already done by software.

Nevada's race book rules require anyone acting as race book manager or supervisor to register with the Gaming Control Board, so oversight of wagering records is tied to an accountable, registered person.

Nevada Regulation 22 covers how wagers are accepted, how winners are paid and how computerised bookmaking systems are used. Records are produced in approved systems that an agent could only reach if the operator granted access.

Camp management platforms such as CampDoc store participants' allergies, medical needs and accommodation details in digital profiles. An agent could pull these together and turn them into staff briefings.

Regpack keeps one profile per camper with health data, forms and group assignments. Group-specific needs are already in systems an agent can reach, which supports end-to-end drafting and sending of briefings.

AI communication and accessibility tools for special-needs populations exist, but no recreation-specific AI product for staff briefings was found. Delivering the briefing in person and judging group sensitivities still rest with the supervisor.

AI onboarding and training tools already draft training modules, keep onboarding consistent across hires, and answer new-hire policy questions around the clock. That covers the explaining-policies part and the preparation of training materials.
AI agents can act as digital coaches that guide frontline workers in real time and personalise their training content. They support the training but do not replace hands-on supervision.

Recreation and aquatics training includes site-specific policy training, skills demonstrations and in-service drills. These need a supervisor present to demonstrate and check the skills, and the training has to be documented.

evidence.fact: Processing means attaching a stainless steel drum to the drive unit, taking off the lid, loading the bone fragments by hand and running the blades, which take about 30 seconds or less. Every step is physical.

Before grinding, metal has to be sifted out by hand because the high-speed rotor would be damaged by it. A magnet misses gold, copper and aluminum parts, so the sorting needs hands and eyes on the remains.

Operators move the remains to a tray, run them under a magnet, pick out implants and joints by hand, then put the bone through the processor. A software-only agent with no robotics cannot do any of this.

Onboarding platforms already generate whole training courses, with sections and lessons, from a single topic prompt. That covers the material-drafting part of training without step-by-step human work.

Vendors sell AI agents for government onboarding that claim to produce onboarding materials and track required training and certifications. These are unverified marketing claims, so I read them only as signs of partial automation of coordination.

Guidance on court staff training says role-specific, hands-on instruction and supervision are still delivered by people. In practice, clerks teach judges and colleagues directly, which points to human-led live training and coordination.

Central issuance software takes card requests from the bank's card management system and sends print jobs to card printers in branches. The data and job steps are digital and an agent could do them, but the printing itself happens on local hardware.

Instant issuance covers data preparation, magnetic stripe encoding, embossing, and chip or contactless personalization. Data preparation can be automated, but embossing and encoding produce a physical card.

Vericast's SaaS platform personalizes EMV chip and dual-interface cards in the branch in about a minute. A person still has to load card stock, take out the finished card, inspect it and hand it over or mail it.
Duck Creek launched Agentic FNOL in Sept 2026. It uses coordinated AI agents to process claims information from digital, mobile and voice channels, targeting manual entry and incomplete data.

Vendor guides describe AI agents that capture loss details, look up policies, and open and update real claim records in core systems such as Guidewire, Duck Creek and Snapsheet. Coverage decisions are left to licensed adjusters. These are vendor claims, not independent measurements.

A 2008 New York DFS legal opinion treats data entry and processing as ministerial work that needs no adjuster license. Only discretionary acts such as loss evaluation and payment authorization require one. Rules vary by state.

Herd-I's commercial dairy system films each cow as she leaves the milking shed and uses cloud models trained by veterinary experts to score lameness and send dashboard alerts. This covers only one narrow part of the task and needs camera hardware installed on the farm.

A Queensland government prototype camera system for beef cattle is being trained to alert producers to injuries, lameness or emergency disease symptoms. It was still in development, not widely deployed.

University research on gait images from depth cameras reports detecting dairy-cow lameness with 99% or higher accuracy. Lameness is the most developed use case, and wider detection of illness and unusual behavior still mostly depends on in-person observation in barns, pens and pastures.

2026 AI agents (Intelinair AGMRI, GROWMARK myFS Agronomy) combine field-level soil, weather, imagery, input-application and yield data to support decisions on nitrogen timing, fungicide use and replanting. GROWMARK says its agent is meant to support crop specialists, not replace them.
The Taranis Ag Assistant is a generative AI tool that draws on in-season crop intelligence, weather maps, machinery data and university research to give agronomic answers to producers.

In California, anyone recommending agricultural pesticide use needs a PCA licence. Property operators and their employees making recommendations for land they control are exempt, so an internal discussion between a supervisor and managers does not require a licensed human signature.

Driverless tractors such as John Deere's autonomous 8R/9RX tillage system rely on machine-mounted cameras, GPS and the vehicle's own robotic hardware, started and monitored from the Operations Center app. That is physical robotics, not the software-only agent this rating assumes. A software agent could at most help with route or field planning.

Driving a truck or tractor on public roads requires a licensed human driver. Farm vehicle operators still need a valid driver's license, though states may waive the CDL requirement under 49 CFR 383.3(d).

John Deere's autonomous tractor is a dedicated robotic machine controlled through a smartphone app, with live video and metrics. It cannot be done by a general-purpose software agent working only through digital systems.

AI planning agents in farm platforms such as Granular and Trimble Ag can weigh field readiness, equipment availability and storage capacity to suggest harvest windows and logistics. That covers the prep work for the meeting, but the meeting itself is still between people.

In 2026, agentic AI in agriculture is mostly used for field operations, fertility prescriptions and directing autonomous equipment. No product was found that handles the supervisor-manager talks on labor schedules or production requirements.
Even with growing interest in AI for farm workforce management, there is still a clear gap between the tools on offer and what farms actually use.

Commercial greenhouse control software, such as AgriLogiq's ZoneLogiq, already handles climate and irrigation control, real-time alerts and remote monitoring. That covers the digital side: diagnosing faults and adjusting setpoints. The physical repair still has to be done by a person.
In farmworker job postings, irrigation repair means hands-on work in the field, such as replacing sprinkler heads and drive chains. An agent with no body cannot do this.
Texas requires a license to repair irrigation systems, but it exempts work on commercial agricultural irrigation systems. No licence barrier was found for farmworkers doing this repair.

Getting a cold frame ready means digging out topsoil by hand, sifting it through wire screen to remove grass and rocks, loosening the subsoil with a pitchfork and working in compost. All of this is manual work done on site.
Hotbeds heated with manure are dug 16 to 24 inches deep and cold frames 6 to 15 inches deep. The pit is filled with manure and then about a foot of soil, which also requires physical labor.

Before sowing, the soil surface is raked and leveled and weeds are removed. The only parts that can be done digitally, such as looking up soil mixes or temperature guidance, are a tiny share of the working time.

Dedicated marine autopilot and autonomy systems, such as Robosys VOYAGER AI SMARTPILOT (waypoint tracking, route following, collision avoidance) and Simrad AutoCaptain, already handle some steering. But they are built-in onboard systems. Simrad AutoCaptain is described as an assisted system that helps the operator, so a human still runs the boat. A general software AI agent would only help with planning routes and reading charts, weather and AIS data.
Simrad AutoCaptain, shown at CES 2026, is an assisted system for docking, low-speed maneuvering and route planning. The operator stays in charge.

Navigation watches on larger fishing vessels are expected to include a licensed deck officer and a lookout. In Washington State this is a voluntary standard for vessels of 300 gross tons and up, not a confirmed federal rule. The person in charge of the vessel answers for its safe navigation.

Software only monitors traps after they have been set: cellular or LoRaWAN devices report when a trap closes, and some use AI to identify the species caught. Choosing, baiting and setting the traps and laying the poison on trails is still physical work done by people in the field.
Wildlife toxicants such as 1080 and strychnine need a state permit plus pesticide applicator certification. In the US, restricted-use pesticides require a certified applicator under 40 CFR 171.
About 23 US states require a wildlife control operator license, and the Canadian job bank says a provincial pesticide applicator licence is required in all provinces.

The Idaho trapper course tells trappers to kill trapped animals in person, with a .22 firearm or a small club struck at the base of the skull. Both methods mean being physically at the trap and handling the animal or a weapon, which a software-only agent cannot do.

Washington requires trapped wild animals to be killed or released immediately. Anyone buying a trapping license for the first time must pass an exam on humane trapping technique, so the person doing the trapping must be a licensed human.

Wisconsin requires live furbearers taken in season to be released unharmed or killed immediately. California bill analysis says animals should be shot where permitted and bars drowning, chest crushing and non-euthanasia chemicals, which shows the methods themselves are regulated.

AI on fishing vessels in 2026 does only digital support work, such as reviewing electronic-monitoring video to count catch, and human reviewers still check its results. The harvesting itself is done by hand: diving, dredging, setting traps and working rods and tackle.
Commercial harvest needs fishery-specific federal and state permits held by eligible persons or entities, plus vessel monitoring and logbooks. That ties the work to licensed humans and vessels.

EU projects pairing AI cameras with robotic arms for catch monitoring are still in research (OptiFish, 2024-2028). They involve robotics, which the reference agents do not have, and they monitor the catch rather than harvest it.

Cutting, notching and boring framing members for pipes is hands-on work that the code limits: hole diameter at most one-third of joist depth, hole edge at least 5/8 inch from the stud edge, notches no deeper than 25% in bearing studs. A worker has to measure and cut on site with tools. Software can only look up these limits.

Retrofit cutting during re-piping must stay within code limits. Cutting into shear walls may need a building permit, and changes to engineered lumber need manufacturer approval or a registered design professional.
Almost all US states license journeyman and master plumbers, and apprentices work under supervision, so licensed humans must perform plumbing work.

ALLDATA Diagnostic Intelligence is an AI-assisted tool. Starting from a trouble code or a symptom, it returns ranked probable causes, OEM diagnostic procedures, shortcut tests, technical service bulletins (TSBs) and wiring diagrams. This means software already does the main lookup and sequencing sub-steps of planning a repair procedure.

Mitchell 1 ProDemand takes the technician from a trouble code or component search straight to test procedures, specifications and diagrams. A browsing or computer-use agent can operate this kind of shop software the technician already has access to.

Judgment call, not a sourced fact: the plan depends on what the technician finds on the physical vehicle and on hands-on experience (seized parts, condition of the vehicle, shop equipment). So a human still has to supply observations and review or adjust the agent's draft before using it. In most US jurisdictions no licence or signature is required to plan the work.

OSHA 29 CFR 1926.451(f)(7) says scaffolds may be erected, moved, dismantled or altered only under the supervision of a competent person, and only by trained workers that person selects. Setting up a scaffold is physical, on-site work that a human is legally responsible for, and it also involves hands-on hazard inspection.
An OSHRC enforcement case issued a serious citation because a scaffold was put up with no competent person present or supervising. This confirms that a human has to be on site.

Scaffold safety programs require physical inspections and erection by trained people. Software agents with no robotics can only help on the side, for example by pulling up checklists or manufacturer instructions.

In 2026, fleet driver-monitoring products (Netradyne, Motive, Fleetx) use AI dashcams to give real-time alerts for speeding, tailgating, distraction and extra passengers. Seatbelt detection appears in fewer products and is still in beta for some. These systems only alert. The licensed human driver still has to drive lawfully and make passengers comply.

In some places the law makes the driver personally responsible for passengers' seat belt use. Since 2013, Hawaii cites the driver if any passenger is unbelted, so legal responsibility sits with the licensed human operator.

Whether the driver must make adult passengers belt up varies by jurisdiction. In the UK the driver is responsible only for themselves and for children. Where it applies, the driver does it in person inside the vehicle, by asking and persuading passengers.

A CRS report dated August 2026 says remote-control technologies are readily available but are not a fully autonomous train control system. Long-haul U.S. freight still has no driverless operation, and crews remain responsible for watching for obstacles because PTC handles only a few types of emergencies.

Locomotive automation pilots such as DB Cargo's ATO/RTO trial and Wabtec Teleops use dedicated onboard hardware with a driver aboard or a remote team ready to take control. General-purpose software agents cannot reach or control the cab.
Under 49 CFR Part 240, each railroad must run an FRA-approved program to certify the locomotive engineers who operate its trains, so a qualified human has to be at the controls.

Ramp agent job postings require lifting up to 70 lbs, often in the cramped aircraft hold, and carrying baggage up and down jet-way stairs. One aircraft can mean more than 100 items, so the core of the task is physical work.

AI weight-and-balance software such as CHAMP Cargospot Autoload can build a cargo load plan in seconds. That is planning, though, not moving the bags, which is only a small part of the attendant's job. The timing figures come from the vendor and have not been independently checked.
Job postings also mention pushing and pulling loaded carts and working outdoors in all weather. A software-only agent with no body or robot cannot do any of that.

Commercial cold-chain platforms such as Emerson GO, ThingsBoard and ITRI stream temperature and humidity sensor data to the cloud. They send threshold alerts in real time and generate compliance reports automatically, so an agent could do the review and flagging work end to end when sensors are installed.

The FDA sanitary transportation rule accepts several ways to show temperature: manual periodic readings, reefer downloads, data loggers or telematics. Records must be auditable, so some checks still rely on physical readings or on downloads taken on site.

Under the rule the shipper sets the required conditions and carriers must show they met them when asked. An inspector's on-site check and sign-off therefore remains a human step where no sensors are installed or readings are disputed.

Commercial and research AI tools such as the OpenGrants AI Grant Writer Agent and GRAIL (IJCAI 2026) can already find grants and write first drafts. Industry guides say AI output is still a starting draft that a human checks, edits and submits. Fully autonomous tools that find, draft and submit applications are still early prototypes.

For EPA Brownfields grants, the organization must have an active SAM.gov registration and UEI. An Authorized Organization Representative approved by the organization's E-Business Point of Contact must submit the application through Grants.gov, so a named human has to submit and certify it.

EPA's Brownfields guidance (FY23 FAQs and the Grants.gov tip sheet) says the AOR must submit the complete application package. Applications are rejected if the SAM.gov account is inactive, which sets institutional and accountability limits on full delegation.
